messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 36
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Accountant
  trauma_type: Witnessed domestic violence (childhood)
  pcl5: 69

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Threat: Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
  Memory: Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words., Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
  Negative Appraisals: No Accountability: The people responsible have faced no consequences, Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable., Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Rajan Mehta is a 36-year-old South Asian man who works as an accountant at a mid-sized firm in the Chicago suburbs. He came to the clinic alone, dressed carefully, speaking in measured sentences that occasionally broke apart mid-thought. He has been divorced for two years. He described his childhood home as a place where, on most evenings, the air changed before anything happened — a particular quality of silence, a shift in his father's posture — and then the violence would begin. From roughly age six through his early teens, Rajan witnessed his father assault his mother repeatedly: thrown objects, hands raised, his mother's body against the kitchen wall while Rajan stood in the hallway or crouched at the top of the stairs, unable to intervene, unable to look away. He was the eldest of three children. He remembered feeling that his smallness was a kind of betrayal — that he should have been able to stop it and could not. His father faced no legal consequences, no formal reckoning of any kind. The family remained intact. His mother never spoke of it afterward, and neither did anyone else.

Rajan left for university at eighteen and told himself he had left all of it behind. He married in his late twenties. He described his ex-wife as kind, and the marriage as one he slowly made uninhabitable, though he struggled to say exactly how. The divorce was finalised two years ago. He has had little contact with his family since.

The symptoms that brought him to seek help did not announce themselves as connected to his childhood. They crept in through his body first. At work, where Rajan spends long hours in an open-plan office, a colleague raising his voice during a phone call — even in frustration, even about something trivial — can produce in Rajan a physical response that is immediate and total: his chest tightens, his hands go cold, his jaw clamps shut. He does not always know why until several minutes later, and sometimes not at all. He described sitting at his desk afterward with his heart still hammering, feeling certain something terrible was about to happen, though nothing in the room had changed. His body, he said, seems to operate on a frequency he cannot tune out — always scanning, always braced. He sleeps poorly and wakes already tense.

What disturbs him most is what happens when the memories come. They do not arrive gradually. A smell, a shift in light, the particular way a door closes can return him instantly to that hallway — not as a recollection but as something indistinguishable from the present moment. The terror he felt as a child arrives with the memory, unchanged by the intervening decades. And yet when he tries to speak about what he witnessed, the words dissolve. He can gesture at the shape of it, but the experience itself resists language in a way that frightens and humiliates him. He had come to believe this meant something was broken in him specifically — that other people could process and narrate their pasts, and he could not.

He had come to believe other things too. That happiness was something that had belonged to an earlier version of himself and had been quietly taken from him without his consent. That the people who had shaped the worst years of his life had moved through the world entirely unburdened by what they had done. And underneath both of these, something more corrosive: that bad things would continue to find him regardless of what he did, that he had no meaningful power to alter the course of his own life.

What finally brought him in was a performance review at work. His manager noted, gently, that Rajan had become increasingly withdrawn from the team over the past year — that he no longer joined meetings he wasn't required to attend, that colleagues found him hard to reach. Rajan had not realised how far he had contracted. He sat in his car afterward for a long time. He said he did not want to keep shrinking. What he hopes for, though he offered it cautiously, is the possibility of feeling like himself again — whoever that was.
